Welcome, and why databases exist

Good morning, and welcome to IT 505, Fundamentals of Database Technologies. This first hour has three lessons of twenty minutes. In the first we agree on how the course runs: the format of a class, the calendar, the grading and the ground rules, and I ask for your written agreement to a format that is mostly online. In the second we look at the database environment: what data and information are, what goes wrong when a business keeps its data in separate files and spreadsheets, and what a database management system does about it. In the third we classify the databases of this course into five families, so that every later class has its place on one diagram.

Each lesson runs the same five beats. I teach for about ten minutes, we look at one diagram or one running example, you do a four-minute exercise, we fix the terms with flashcards, and we take a two-minute break. Nothing in this hour is graded.

The one fact to remember

One project carries the whole course. Mercadillo 505 is a fictional online market in Madrid whose orders arrive as one flat file of about 2,000 lines. In the studio you will store those same orders in a file-based database, in a relational database, as documents, as key-value pairs, as a graph, as a columnar big-data file and as a hash-chained ledger. The three labs are stages of that project, and the Mid-term and the Final ask you to do what the labs made you practise.

By the end of this hour you will be able to

  1. State how the course runs — the format of a class, the calendar with the two exam days on campus, the grading weights and the ground rules — and give your written agreement to that format.
  2. Distinguish data, information and decision, and define database, DBMS (Database Management System) and database application.
  3. Name five problems of keeping business data in separate files and spreadsheets, and the responsibility of a DBMS that answers each one.
  4. Name the four roles that work with databases and say what each one does.
  5. Classify a data need into one of the five families of databases of this course, and justify the choice in one sentence.
Lab 1 — Build: from a flat file to a relational database — opens today, due Sunday 6 December 2026 at 23:59. The three real-life examples of this lecture return in the labs: the five planning questions are the model of Lab 1, Step 0; the problem list of the order sheet is the first deliverable of Lab 1, Step 1; the family table is the template of the Lab 3 memo.

Teach — lesson notes (10 minutes)

Slide 7 · Who is in the room

Who is in the room

Before the course, the people. In a moment each of you will say three things: your name, what you studied or worked in before this programme, and one data headache you have had. A data headache is any moment when data did not behave as expected: a spreadsheet that existed in two versions and nobody knew which one was correct, a report whose totals did not match the source, a file that opened with broken characters. Keep it to one sentence. I will write the headaches on the board, because by the end of Lesson 2 you will be able to name the cause of most of them in technical terms. I will start with my own.

Slide 8 · What this course is about

What this course is about

This course is about one question: where and how should a business keep its data, so that the data can be trusted and used for decisions? A database is an organised collection of logically related data, and the course teaches you to design one, to build one and to query one.

The syllabus sets five learning outcomes. In plain words: first, you see how the analysis of data changes the efficiency and the productivity of a firm. Second, you can explain what a well-designed database is, compare approaches and choose the appropriate one for a business situation. Third, you can write and read SQL (Structured Query Language), the language used to define, change and query the data of a relational database. Fourth, you can work out which data a business analysis needs and obtain them with SQL queries. Fifth, you can apply big-data analytics to business situations with a scientific approach.

You are data scientists in training. Most of the data you will ever analyse is stored in a database before it reaches your notebook, and SQL is how you get it out. No previous knowledge of databases is assumed.

Slide 9 · How one class runs

How one class runs

Every class has the same shape. The first hour is the lecture, and it is never one long talk: it is cut into three parts of twenty minutes, or into four parts of fifteen minutes when there is more to cover. Each part has five beats, always in the same order. Teach: a short lesson on one topic. See: a diagram, an animation or a live demonstration of the same idea. Do: a short practical exercise. Keep: flashcards or a short quiz that fix the terms in memory, and are never graded. Breathe: a two-minute break.

The next two hours are the studio: guided practice on a shared reference database, a real break, and then the same skill applied to your own project, which is lab work. After class comes the home sprint: personal work that finishes what the studio started, with lab work first, then a short reading, then the flashcard deck of the day.

Slide 10 · The calendar: fourteen classes in four weeks

The calendar: fourteen classes in four weeks

The course has fourteen class meetings, from Monday to Thursday, between Monday 23 November and Thursday 17 December 2026. Classes 1 to 5 are on campus: the four days of this week, and Monday 30 November. Tuesday 1 December is a self-paced online day: there is no live session, you work through four short lessons, and a short check-in that you hand in by 23:59 counts as your attendance. From Wednesday 2 December the classes are live online. There is no class on Monday 7 and Tuesday 8 December.

Two days are different, and they are the two days you must plan now. Thursday 3 December is the Mid-term exam and Thursday 17 December is the Final exam. Both are held on campus, in person, and both are invigilated by another professor.

Slide 12 · How you are graded

How you are graded

The syllabus fixes three weights. Continuous work counts for 30 per cent of the course grade, the Mid-term for 30 per cent and the Final for 40 per cent. Continuous work is the three labs and a small number of class challenges. The Mid-term covers Classes 1 to 6; the Final covers the whole course, with more weight on the second half. Both exams contain theory questions and application problems, some of them at the computer, and both are taken in the Respondus LockDown Browser, a browser that blocks every other application while an exam is open. You will install it and test it before the Mid-term.

The course grade is the weighted sum of the three components, and the syllabus converts it to a letter: 93 and above is an A, 83 to 86 is a B, 73 to 76 is a C. The complete scale is in the reference tables of this module. The quizzes and flashcards inside the lectures are formative: they give you feedback, and they do not count.

Slide 13 · Three labs, one project

Three labs, one project

The continuous work is built on three labs. Lab 1, Build, opens today and is due on Sunday 6 December at 23:59: you take a flat file and turn it into a relational database. Lab 2, Ask, opens on Monday 30 November and is due on Sunday 13 December: you answer business questions in SQL. Lab 3, Choose, is the short one. It opens on Wednesday 9 December and is due on Sunday 20 December: you try one non-relational, big-data or ledger tool, and you recommend the right database for one business situation.

Labs are done alone or in pairs. All three use the same case, Mercadillo 505, or a dataset of your own if I approve it this week. A dataset of your own needs an open licence that you can name, no personal information about real people, and at least 1,000 rows that describe at least three kinds of thing. Every tool in the course is open-source software, and each one can be replaced by another suitable tool if you can justify the choice.

Slide 14 · Ground rules

Ground rules

Three rules protect everyone in this room. First, no recording: classes, studios and online meetings are not recorded, photographed or screen-captured without written permission. This protects the privacy of your classmates as well as the course materials. Second, honest work: what you hand in is your own work or your pair's, your sources are cited in APA (American Psychological Association) style, and the rules on collaboration and on automated tools are written on each lab sheet. The University's Academic Honesty Policy applies in full.

Third, fictional or open data only: the labs use invented data, or datasets published under an open licence. You never load personal information about real people — customers, colleagues, patients, friends — into a course database. In the European Union such data are protected by the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), and a classroom laptop is not a controlled environment. The full terms are in the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy; the link is on the slide and at the bottom of every page of this module.

Lesson 2 — The database environment
Data, information, decision — files and spreadsheets and where they hurt — database, DBMS (Database Management System), application — what a DBMS promises — who works with databases

Teach — lesson notes (10 minutes)
Slide 20 · Data, information, decision
Data, information, decision
A business does not want data; it wants to decide. To see the difference we need three precise terms. Data are recorded representations of facts — numbers, text, dates, images — in a formalised form that can be stored, transmitted and processed. The line 'M505-1041, 21 November 2026, Madrid, olive oil one litre, 9.80, 2' is data. Information is data that has been processed and placed in a context, so that it has a meaning for the person who receives it: 'on Saturday 21 November, Madrid produced 67 per cent of the revenue'. A decision is a choice between actions that is taken on the basis of information: 'next Saturday the second delivery van goes to Madrid'.
The direction matters. Decisions depend on information, information is computed from data, and therefore an error in the data becomes an error in the decision. One more term completes the set. Metadata are data that describe other data: the name of a column, its type, its unit, the rule that a quantity must be greater than zero. Without metadata the value 9.80 cannot be interpreted: nobody can tell whether it is a price in euros or a weight in kilograms.
Slide 21 · Life before databases: files and spreadsheets
Life before databases: files and spreadsheets
Before database software existed, and in many small businesses still today, each department kept its own files, and each program read and wrote its own file in its own format. This is called a file-processing system. Its usual form today is the spreadsheet: one file for orders, a second one for customers, a third that someone copied on Friday and corrected on Monday. A spreadsheet is a good calculating tool for one person. It stores whatever is typed into a cell, it does not check a value against any rule unless somebody builds that check by hand, and it has no reliable way to let two people change the same file at the same time.
Slide 22 · Five problems of separate files
Five problems of separate files
The textbook lists the consequences, and you will recognise your own data headaches in them. One: data redundancy — the same fact is stored in more than one place, for example a customer's city in the orders file and in the customers file. Two: data inconsistency — the copies stop agreeing, because one was updated and the other was not, or because the same city is typed 'Madrid' in one row and 'MADRID' in capital letters in another. Three: program-data dependence — the description of the data is written inside each program or each formula, so that adding one column forces every program and every formula that reads the file to be changed. Four: limited data sharing — each file belongs to one person or one department, and two people who save the same file at the same moment overwrite each other's changes. Five: no enforced rules — nothing prevents an empty quantity, a negative price or a duplicated row. Each of the five makes the information computed from the files unreliable.
ProblemWhat happensAt Mercadillo 505
1 · Data redundancyThe same fact is stored in more than one placeA customer's city in the orders file and in the customers file
2 · Data inconsistencyThe copies stop agreeing'Madrid' in one row, 'MADRID' in another
3 · Program-data dependenceThe description of the data is written inside each program or formulaOne new column: every formula that reads the file must be changed
4 · Limited data sharingEach file has one owner; simultaneous saves overwrite each otherTwo assistants save the same sheet at the same moment
5 · No enforced rulesNothing prevents an impossible valueAn empty quantity, a negative price, a duplicated row
Slide 23 · Database, DBMS (Database Management System), application: who does what
Database, DBMS (Database Management System), application: who does what
The database approach answers these problems by separating three things that a spreadsheet mixes. The database is the organised collection of logically related data, stored together with its metadata. The DBMS is the software that creates the database, keeps it up to date and controls every access to it: no user and no program reads or writes the stored data directly; every request goes through the DBMS. A database application is a program that carries out a specific task for its users — taking an order, printing an invoice, drawing a sales chart — by sending requests to the DBMS.
Many applications and many users can work with the same database at the same time, because the DBMS stands between them and the data. And because the description of the data is stored once, in the database itself, a change in the structure does not have to be repeated in every program. This property is called program-data independence. In this course PostgreSQL, SQLite and DuckDB are the DBMS products; DBeaver is the application through which you send them requests; and the request language is SQL (Structured Query Language).
Slide 24 · Schematic 2 — The database environment
Slide 25 · What a DBMS (Database Management System) promises (1/2)
What a DBMS promises (1/2)
A DBMS takes on a small number of responsibilities, and each one removes one of the problems of the previous slide. The first is persistence: once the DBMS has confirmed a change, the change is on durable storage and is still there after the program closes or the power fails. The second is data integrity: the accuracy and consistency of the stored data. The designer declares rules, called constraints — this column may not be empty, this value must be unique, this quantity must be greater than zero, this order must refer to a customer that exists. The DBMS checks them at every insertion and at every change, and it refuses a row that breaks one. The rule is declared once, and it applies to every user and to every application.
Slide 26 · What a DBMS (Database Management System) promises (2/2)
What a DBMS promises (2/2)
The third responsibility is concurrency control: many users can read and change the same data at the same time, and the DBMS orders their operations so that no change is lost and nobody reads a half-finished change. The unit of work is the transaction, a group of operations that is carried out completely or not at all; Class 4 covers it under the name ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). The fourth is security: the DBMS identifies each user and allows only the operations that this user has been granted. The fifth is backup and recovery: the DBMS can copy the database and restore it to a correct state after a failure.
The sixth is a query language. Instead of writing a program for each question, the user states which data are wanted, and the DBMS works out how to retrieve them. For relational databases that language is SQL, standardised by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) and IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission) as ISO/IEC 9075.
Slide 27 · Who works with databases
Who works with databases
Four roles work with databases, and one person often holds more than one of them. The data analyst turns business questions into queries and presents the answers as tables and charts. The data scientist builds statistical and machine-learning models; the data for those models are selected, joined and summarised in the database before they are loaded into Python or R, so SQL is part of the job. The data engineer builds and operates the processes that move data from the systems where they are produced into the databases where they are analysed. The DBA (database administrator) installs the DBMS, controls access, makes backups and keeps performance acceptable. In the labs you will take all four roles in turn, on a small scale.
Key terms to learn
data
recorded representations of facts in a formalised form that can be stored, transmitted and processed
information
data processed and placed in a context, so that it has a meaning for the person who receives it
decision
a choice between actions, taken on the basis of information
metadata
data that describe other data: names, types, units, rules
file-processing system
an arrangement in which each program keeps its own files in its own format
data redundancy
the same fact stored in more than one place
data inconsistency
copies of the same fact that no longer agree
program-data dependence / independence
the description of the data written inside each program / stored once, in the database
database
an organised collection of logically related data, stored together with its metadata
DBMS (Database Management System)
the software that creates a database, keeps it up to date and controls every access to it
database application
a program that carries out a task for its users by sending requests to the DBMS
persistence
confirmed changes remain on durable storage after the program closes or the power fails
data integrity · constraint
the accuracy and consistency of the stored data · a declared rule that the DBMS checks at every change
concurrency control · transaction
safe simultaneous use by many users · a group of operations carried out completely or not at all
query language
a language in which the user states which data are wanted; for relational databases, SQL (Structured Query Language)

Where it returns in the labs
The problem list written here — problem, row, effect, rule — is the first deliverable of Lab 1, Step 1 (profile the flat file), where the file has about 2,000 rows instead of ten. The three rules return as the three integrity tests of Lab 1, Step 3, written as real constraints in PostgreSQL. The comparison of totals 'as typed' and 'checked' is the pattern of Lab 2, Part B.
Saturday 21 November 2026 was a busy day at Mercadillo 505. On Monday morning Carmen, the manager of the market, asks a simple question: how many orders did each city place on Saturday, and how much revenue did each city bring? She needs the answer to decide where the second delivery van goes next Saturday. Two assistants open the same sheet and report different numbers. The sheet has ten rows and three problems. Every name in it is invented.

As typed, the sheet says: Madrid 39.10 €, Getafe 24.80 €, Alcobendas 10.80 €, and a fourth 'city', MADRID, with 6.90 €. After the three corrections — the duplicate removed, the spelling agreed, the quantity confirmed with the customer as 2 — it says: Madrid 56.80 €, Getafe 17.30 €, Alcobendas 10.80 €. As typed, Madrid brings about one and a half times the revenue of Getafe; checked, it brings more than three times as much. The second van goes to Madrid, and the decision is taken on numbers that everybody can reproduce.

Keep — five flash-cards (click a card to see its answer)
What are data?click to flip
Recorded representations of facts — numbers, text, dates — in a formalised form that can be stored, transmitted and processed. By themselves they contain no conclusion.click to flip back
What is information?click to flip
Data that have been processed and placed in a context, so that they have a meaning for the person who receives them. A decision is taken on the basis of information.click to flip back
What is a database?click to flip
An organised collection of logically related data, stored together with its metadata (the description of the data: names, types, units, rules).click to flip back
What is a DBMS (Database Management System)?click to flip
The software that creates the database, keeps it up to date and controls every access to it. No user and no program reads or writes the stored data directly.click to flip back
What is data integrity, and how does a DBMS (Database Management System) protect it?click to flip
The accuracy and consistency of the stored data. The designer declares constraints; the DBMS (Database Management System) checks them at every insertion and change and refuses a row that breaks one.click to flip back

Lesson 3 — The map: five families of databases
Flat and file-based — relational — non-relational — big data — blockchain — and what 'open source' means in this course

Teach — lesson notes (10 minutes)
Slide 32 · Why there is more than one kind of database
Why there is more than one kind of database
There is no single best database. A database is designed for a certain shape of data and for a certain kind of question, and it is weaker outside that design. Four properties of the data need decide the choice. The structure of the data: identical fields in every record, or records that differ from each other. The typical question: one record found by its identifier, a summary over millions of rows, or a path through relationships. The number of writers: one person, or thousands of users at the same time. And the volume: what fits on one machine, or more. This course groups the systems into five families. For each family I name its data model, the open-source products we use, and the class in which we work with it.
Slide 33 · Family 1 — Flat and file-based
Family 1 — Flat and file-based
The first family is the simplest. A flat file is a single file that holds one table and nothing else: no rules, no declared types, no links to other files. The most common format is CSV (Comma-Separated Values): one record per line, with the values separated by commas. Flat files are the standard way to exchange data between programs, and the Mercadillo 505 starter file is one.
A file-based database, also called an embedded database, is a complete DBMS (Database Management System) that runs inside the program that uses it and keeps the whole database in one ordinary file. There is no server to install or to start. We use two of them. SQLite stores data row by row and is built for many small reads and writes; its authors have placed it in the public domain. DuckDB stores data column by column and is built for analysis; it can query a CSV file directly, without loading it first. We work with this family in Class 2.
Slide 34 · Family 2 — Relational
Family 2 — Relational
The second family takes most of our time. In a relational database all data are held in tables. A table has columns, each with a name and one data type, and rows, each describing one thing. Every table has a primary key, a column or a set of columns whose value identifies each row uniquely, and tables are linked by foreign keys, columns whose values must match a primary key in another table. The model was published in 1970 by Edgar F. Codd, a researcher at IBM (International Business Machines), and the language used with it, SQL (Structured Query Language), has been an international standard since 1987.
A relational DBMS enforces constraints and supports transactions. That is why it is the usual choice when many users change related data that must remain correct: orders, payments, stock, enrolments. Our relational DBMS is PostgreSQL, which is published under an open-source licence; MariaDB is a second open-source system of the same family. The syllabus names Microsoft SQL Server. It is a commercial relational DBMS, the SQL you learn here applies to it, and every SQL class carries a one-line note on the differences. Classes 3 to 10 are relational.
Slide 35 · Family 3 — Non-relational (1/2): documents and key-value pairs
Family 3 — Non-relational (1/2): documents and key-value pairs
The third family groups the systems that do not use tables linked by keys. The common name is NoSQL (not only SQL). There are four kinds. A document database stores each record as one self-contained document, usually in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) format. A document can contain lists and nested parts, and two documents in the same collection need not have the same fields. An order together with its lines can be a single document. Open-source examples are Apache CouchDB and FerretDB.
A key-value store holds pairs: a unique key, and a value that the system does not interpret. It answers one request very fast — give me the value for this key — and little else. A shopping cart held under the visitor's session identifier is the typical case. Our example is Valkey.
Slide 36 · Family 3 — Non-relational (2/2): wide columns and graphs
Family 3 — Non-relational (2/2): wide columns and graphs
A wide-column store keeps rows that are found by a key, and each row may hold a different and very large set of columns. The rows are distributed over many machines, and the tables are designed around the queries that will be asked. It is used for very large volumes of writes, such as histories of events. The open-source example is Apache Cassandra.
A graph database stores nodes, which represent things, and relationships between nodes; both can have properties. It is built for questions about connections: who referred whom, which products are bought together, which is the shortest route between two points. Examples are Neo4j Community Edition and Apache AGE, an extension that adds graph queries to PostgreSQL. Non-relational systems are usually chosen for flexibility of structure or for distribution over many machines, and many of them accept weaker guarantees of consistency in exchange. We work with them in Class 11.
Slide 37 · Family 4 — Big data
Family 4 — Big data
The fourth family is defined by size, not by a data model. Data are called big data when their volume, the speed at which they arrive, or their variety exceeds what one machine can store and process in an acceptable time. Two techniques answer this. The first is columnar storage: a file format such as Apache Parquet stores the values of each column together and compresses them, so a query that needs three columns out of fifty reads only those three. The second is distributed processing: an engine such as Apache Spark splits a large job into tasks, runs the tasks on many machines in parallel and combines the partial results. The questions are still written in SQL, or in a data-frame notation that is close to it. For data that still fit on one laptop, DuckDB reads Parquet files directly. Class 12 covers this family.
Slide 38 · Family 5 — Blockchain
Family 5 — Blockchain
The fifth family is the blockchain, a kind of distributed ledger. A ledger is a record of transactions to which entries are added and never changed. In a blockchain the entries are grouped into blocks. Each block contains a hash of the previous block: a short value of fixed length, computed from the entire content of that block by a hash function. If anyone alters an old entry, the hash of its block changes, the value stored in the next block no longer matches, and the alteration is detected. This property is called tamper evidence.
Copies of the ledger are held by many independent participants, who follow a consensus procedure to agree on each new block, so no single participant controls the record. The price is low speed and a high cost in storage and energy, compared with an ordinary database. A blockchain is appropriate only when several organisations that do not fully trust each other must share one record. Bitcoin and Ethereum are public blockchains; Hyperledger Fabric is an open-source platform for blockchains whose participants are known. Class 12 covers it.
Slide 39 · What 'open source' means in this course
What 'open source' means in this course
Every tool in this course is open-source software, and the term has a precise meaning. The OSI (Open Source Initiative) maintains the Open Source Definition: the licence must allow anyone to use the software for any purpose, to read and to modify its source code, and to redistribute the original or the modified version. A product whose source code can be read is not open source unless its licence grants these rights. This is why the course does not use MongoDB: since 2018 it has been published under the SSPL (Server Side Public License), a licence that the OSI has not approved. Before you choose any tool for a lab, find its licence and look for it on the list of licences approved by the OSI. Checking the licence of a tool is part of the work of a data professional, and Lab 3 asks you to do it in writing.

Key terms to learn
flat file
a single file that holds one table, with no rules, no declared types and no links to other files
CSV (Comma-Separated Values)
a text format with one record per line and the values separated by commas
file-based (embedded) database
a complete DBMS (Database Management System) that runs inside the program that uses it and keeps the database in one file, with no server
relational database
a database in which all data are held in tables linked by keys
table · column · row
the structure of relational data: a column has a name and one data type; a row describes one thing
primary key · foreign key
the value that identifies each row uniquely · a value that must match a primary key in another table
document database
stores each record as one self-contained document, usually in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) format
key-value store
stores pairs of a unique key and a value that the system does not interpret
wide-column store
stores rows found by a key, each with its own set of columns, distributed over many machines
graph database
stores nodes and the relationships between them, for questions about connections
big data
data whose volume, speed of arrival or variety exceeds what one machine can store and process in an acceptable time
columnar storage · distributed processing
the values of each column stored together · one job split into tasks that run on many machines
ledger · block · hash
a record to which entries are only added · a group of entries · a fixed-length value computed from data, which changes when the data change
tamper evidence · consensus
any alteration of past entries is detectable · the procedure by which participants agree on each new block
open-source software
software whose licence allows anyone to use, study, modify and redistribute it; the licences are approved by the OSI (Open Source Initiative)

Real-life example 3 — Seven data needs, five families
Slide 41 · Real-life example 3 — Seven data needs, five families (1/2)Slide 42 · Real-life example 3 — Seven data needs, five families (2/2)
Task
Classify seven everyday systems into the five families by answering the same ordered questions about each one, and justify every choice in one sentence.
How it relates to this lecture
It applies the four deciding properties of this lesson — structure, typical question, number of writers, volume — and it places one system in every family and in three of the four non-relational kinds.
Where it returns in the labs
This is the reasoning of Lab 3 (Choose: the right database for the job). Its one-page memo compares PostgreSQL with one other system on four points and ends with a three-sentence recommendation; the table below — system, deciding property, family, justification — is the template of that memo. System 1, the flat export, is the starting point of Lab 1.
The five systems of the Do activity come from daily life: a bank, a shopping cart, a social network, a sensor feed and a land registry. Two more complete the set, so that every family is used: the monthly export that a shop sends to its accountant, which is where Mercadillo 505 starts, and a product catalogue in which each kind of product has different attributes.
SystemWhat is stored, and what is askedDeciding propertyFamilyWhy, in one sentence
1 · Monthly export for the accountantOne table of last month's order lines, read by one personOne table, one reader, no simultaneous writers1 Flat / file-based (a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file; DuckDB to analyse it)Exchanging one table needs no server and no declared rules
2 · A bank's account transfersAccounts and transfers; thousands of users write at once; a transfer must debit one account and credit another togetherIdentical fields in every record; strict transactions2 Relational (PostgreSQL)Related rows must stay correct under many simultaneous writers
3 · A web shop's shopping cartOne small list per visitor, read and replaced as a whole, forgotten after a few hoursOne lookup by one key3 Non-relational: key-value (Valkey)The only question is 'the cart for this session identifier', and it must be fast
4 · A product catalogueA cheese has a weight and a curing time, a jar of honey has a flower and a volume: the attributes differRecords with different, nested fields, read as a whole3 Non-relational: document (Apache CouchDB, FerretDB)Each product is one self-contained document with its own fields
5 · A social networkPeople and 'follows' relationships; 'friends of friends who like X'The question is a path through relationships3 Non-relational: graph (Neo4j Community, Apache AGE)Paths of several steps are the main question
6 · A sensor feed400 sensors, one reading every 10 seconds: about 3.5 million rows a day; summaries over yearsVolume and speed of arrival4 Big data (Apache Parquet, Apache Spark)More than a thousand million rows a year, read column by column for summaries
7 · A land registry shared by several authoritiesProperty titles used by registry offices, notaries, banks and the tax office; past entries must never changeSeveral independent organisations; a history that must not be altered5 Blockchain (Hyperledger Fabric)No single organisation should be able to alter the shared history
Two remarks keep the classification honest. First, the families are not exclusive: one company commonly uses several at the same time — a relational database for its orders, a key-value store for its shopping carts, columnar files for its history. Second, system 7 is the standard textbook candidate for a blockchain, and most land registries nevertheless run on relational databases today; a blockchain is justified only if the authorities really are independent and none of them is trusted to keep the single copy. Class 12 gives a flowchart for that decision.

The code of the example in Python — a comment before every line (click to show or hide)
The complete source of the interactive page (HTML (HyperText Markup Language)) — a comment before every line
Step by step — what the example does
  1. The listing is a Python program of about thirty lines; every line is preceded by a comment. It defines the seven systems as dictionaries of observed facts and one function, choose_family.
  2. Start takes the systems one at a time. For each system the first test asks whether several independent organisations share the record and whether its history must be unalterable: 'yes' ends at blockchain.
  3. The second test asks whether the volume or the speed of arrival exceeds one machine: 'yes' ends at big data. The third asks whether the data are one table with a single writer: 'yes' ends at flat and file-based.
  4. The fourth test asks whether all records have the same fields and whether strict transactions are required: 'yes' ends at relational. Otherwise the main question selects the non-relational kind: by key, whole record, path, or wide rows.
  5. Each test is written to the execution window with the observed value and the branch taken, and the corresponding box of the family map is outlined; the final box is filled.
  6. After the seventh system the results table lists all seven with their family and their one-sentence reason: the same table as in the real-life example.
  7. The Python listing runs as it is with any Python 3 interpreter (it uses no library). In the page, the same tests are carried out by a JavaScript function, because a browser does not run Python.

  • Step 1 — Class 2 — Profile the flat file (the problem list), load it into a file-based database, and answer the questions that one table can answer.
  • Step 2 — Class 3 — Write the business rules, draw the diagram, and write the schema in third normal form.
  • Step 3 — Class 4 — Create the schema in PostgreSQL, load the data, and run three integrity tests in which the database refuses a bad row.
  • Report — by Sunday 6 December, 23:59 — Five pages at most: introduction, body, conclusion; sources in APA (American Psychological Association) style. Hand in the report as PDF (Portable Document Format), schema.sql, load.sql and the diagram as an image.
Lab 1 of 3 — opens Monday 23 November, due Sunday 6 December 2026 at 23:59, alone or in pairs. Tonight only Step 0: choose your data and write five business questions. Every tool named in the labs is open-source software and can be replaced by any other suitable tool that you can justify: research your tools thoroughly, and build your own where that helps.
Textbook: Hoffer, J. A., Venkataraman, R., & Topi, H. (2018). Modern database management (13th ed.). Pearson.

Data, information, decision, metadata (Lesson 2)
TermDefinitionExample at Mercadillo 505
DataRecorded representations of facts in a formalised form that can be stored, transmitted and processedM505-1041, 2026-11-21, Madrid, Olive oil 1 L, 9.80, 2
InformationData processed and placed in a context, so that it has a meaning for the person who receives itMadrid produced 67 % of Saturday's revenue
DecisionA choice between actions, taken on the basis of informationNext Saturday the second delivery van goes to Madrid
MetadataData that describe other data: names, types, units, rulesunit_price is a number with two decimals, in euros, greater than zero
Five problems of separate files, and the answer of the database approach (Lesson 2)
ProblemWhat happensAt Mercadillo 505What the database approach does
Data redundancyThe same fact is stored in more than one placeA customer's city in the orders file and in the customers fileEach fact is stored once and referred to by a key
Data inconsistencyThe copies stop agreeing'Madrid' in one row, 'MADRID' in anotherIntegrity constraints refuse a value that breaks the declared rule
Program-data dependenceThe description of the data is written inside each program or formulaOne new column: every formula that reads the file must be changedProgram-data independence: the structure is described once, in the database
Limited data sharingEach file has one owner; simultaneous saves overwrite each otherTwo assistants save the same sheet at the same momentConcurrency control and security: many users, each with granted rights
No enforced rulesNothing prevents an impossible valueAn empty quantity, a negative price, a duplicated rowNOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE and key constraints, checked at every change
Six responsibilities of a DBMS (Lesson 2)
ResponsibilityWhat the DBMS (Database Management System) guarantees
PersistenceA confirmed change is on durable storage and survives a closed program or a power failure
Data integrityDeclared constraints are checked at every insertion and change; a row that breaks one is refused
Concurrency controlMany users work at the same time; no change is lost and no half-finished change is read
SecurityEach user is identified and may carry out only the operations that have been granted
Backup and recoveryThe database can be copied, and restored to a correct state after a failure
Query languageThe user states which data are wanted and the DBMS works out how to retrieve them (SQL (Structured Query Language), ISO/IEC 9075)
Who works with databases (Lesson 2)
RoleWhat the role does
Data analystTurns business questions into queries and presents the answers as tables and charts
Data scientistBuilds statistical and machine-learning models; selects, joins and summarises the data in the database first
Data engineerBuilds and operates the processes that move data into the databases where they are analysed
Database administratorInstalls the DBMS (Database Management System), controls access, makes backups and keeps performance acceptable

The five families of databases (Lesson 3)
FamilyData modelTypical questionOpen-source products of this courseClass
1 Flat and file-basedOne table in one file (CSV (Comma-Separated Values)); or a complete DBMS (Database Management System) inside the program, the database in one fileExchange one table; analyse it on one computerCSV files · SQLite (public domain) · DuckDB (MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) licence)Class 2
2 RelationalTables of rows and columns, linked by primary and foreign keys; constraints; transactionsMany users change related data that must stay correctPostgreSQL (PostgreSQL Licence) · MariaDB (GPL 2.0)Classes 3 to 10
3 Non-relationalDocuments (JSON (JavaScript Object Notation)) · key-value pairs · wide columns · graphs of nodes and relationshipsThe whole record · the value for a key · very many writes · paths through relationshipsApache CouchDB, FerretDB · Valkey · Apache Cassandra · Neo4j Community, Apache AGEClass 11
4 Big dataColumnar files; one job split over many machinesSummaries over more data than one machine handlesApache Parquet · Apache Spark · DuckDB on one laptopClass 12
5 BlockchainA ledger of blocks, each storing the hash of the previous one; many independent copiesA shared record that no single organisation can alterBitcoin Core, Ethereum (public) · Hyperledger Fabric (known participants)Class 12
Seven everyday systems and their family (Lesson 3)
SystemDeciding propertyFamilyReason
Monthly export for the accountantOne table, one reader, no simultaneous writers1 Flat and file-basedone table, one reader, no simultaneous writers
A bank's account transfersIdentical fields; strict transactions2 Relationalidentical fields and strict transactions under many writers
A web shop's shopping cartMain question: by key3 Non-relational: key-valuethe main question is 'by key'
A product catalogueMain question: whole record3 Non-relational: documentthe main question is 'whole record'
A social networkMain question: path3 Non-relational: graphthe main question is 'path'
A sensor feedVolume or speed of arrival4 Big datathe volume or the speed of arrival exceeds one machine
A land registry shared by several authoritiesIndependent organisations; a history that must not be altered5 Blockchainindependent organisations share a history that must not be altered
